analysis.title: UST Refunding Recap: A shorter kick of the can
key_insights: Treasury left coupon auction sizes unchanged at the November 4, 2026 Quarterly Refunding Announcement (QRA), as RBC expected, despite market chatter about long-end issuance cuts.

Treasury changed its forward guidance by dropping "at least" from "at least several quarters" on holding auction sizes unchanged. RBC says this tightens the timeframe for potential changes. The language has been in refunding statements since February 2024.

RBC reads the guidance change as pointing to coupon increases, consistent with primary dealers and the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee (TBAC) generally expecting increases to be warranted by the end of the fiscal year. The final QRA of FY2027 is August 4, 2027, and RBC sees a high probability the guidance is dropped or fundamentally altered in the next statement.
Some market participants read the change as two-directional, possibly opening the door to long-end auction cuts. RBC sees it entirely in terms of increases.

Markets took the announcement in stride. The long end underperformed, but the belly-led rally was driven mainly by an oil selloff after JD Vance and President Trump acknowledged that Republican underperformance in the midterms was largely driven by the Iran War. The 20-year sector underperformed slightly on the curve, and a post-QRA dip in long-end swap spreads reversed almost immediately.

RBC still expects coupon increases focused in the belly and front end, but has moved the timing from the May 2027 refunding to August 2027. RBC has low conviction on timing because it lacks insight into Treasury's reaction function around bill supply.
RBC does not expect a "twist" (front-end coupon increases paired with back-end cuts). All auction sizes are likely headed higher, or at best staying constant, given expected financing needs.

The debt limit may delay increases further. RBC expects it to become binding early next year, with Treasury possibly under extraordinary measures through the end of FY27. The x-date is likely binary between July/August and late October, depending on whether Treasury lasts to the September 15 corporate tax date. Treasury has historically not increased coupon auctions while the debt limit binds, so August 2027 increases may slip to November or later.

Treasury added a line about engaging market participants on supply and demand dynamics and a statement that it will be guided by financing at the lowest cost over time. RBC sees little directional signal in it.

The 7-year auction cycle will move from monthly to quarterly, mirroring the 10s, 20s and 30s, effective with the March 2027 auction. RBC does not expect total issuance to change, and expects smoother settlement, fewer fails and better netting from fewer, larger CUSIPs.

RBC shifted its near-term bill forecasts after recent bill auction increases and Treasury's financing estimates released Monday. The change is in the timing of cash flows and cash balance assumptions, not in deficit levels. A $33bn HHS outflow for prescription drugs on October 30 was unexpected.

RBC pushed the next bill supply cuts to late November and agrees with Treasury that bill supply must ramp back up in January. It expects the debt limit to bind around mid-March, which clouds the bill outlook after that. No debt-limit paydowns are penciled in yet, and any would likely fall in late spring or early summer.

TBAC found "no clear evidence" that AI/capex-related issuance is crowding out Treasuries. RBC calls it a marginally exacerbating factor in this year's Treasury selloff. A second TBAC presentation covered investor demand for derivative duration versus cash Treasuries, and ideas to lift end-user demand for Treasuries, such as easing balance sheet constraints, changing accounting and tax treatment, and building out repo.

macro_indicators.interpretation: No cuts to long-end issuance, as RBC expected. The long end underperformed modestly but showed no major disappointment.

macro_indicators.reading: First increases pushed from May 2027 to August 2027, focused in belly and front end
macro_indicators.interpretation: The debt limit may delay increases to November 2027 or later. RBC has low conviction on timing.
Treasury likely uses extraordinary measures through the end of FY27. The x-date is likely between July/August and late October.
Bill supply is expected to ramp back up in January. Debt-limit paydowns are not yet included and would likely come in late spring or early summer.
The outflow was unexpected and partly explains why recent bill auction increases exceeded RBC's forecasts.

risk_factors: Debt limit becoming binding early 2027 could delay coupon increases beyond August 2027 and cloud the bill supply outlook after March.
RBC has low conviction on timing of coupon increases because of uncertainty about Treasury's reaction function around bill supply.
Some in the market read the dropped "at least" as opening the door to long-end auction cuts, which RBC does not expect.
The debt limit x-date could be binary between July/August and late October 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Some in the market argued that dropping "at least" from the forward guidance could open the door to long-end auction cuts, which would support long-dated Treasuries.
tension_points.bear_case: RBC reads the change entirely in terms of coupon increases, citing the TBAC discussion and the primary dealer survey. It sees all auction sizes headed higher or, at best, constant.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A reduction in long-end auction sizes at a future refunding would support the cuts view. RBC expects the guidance to be dropped or fundamentally altered at the August 4, 2027 QRA.
